notes.4: The majority of candidates understood how to do this basic ratio question, but some poor arithmetic was seen. Some gave answers which were not whole numbers. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0580 Mathematics June 2015
notes.5: Many correct answers were seen. Some candidates gave the answer as 3 x (3 x – 2 x ). A small number only used 3 or x as the factor.
notes.6: Fewer candidates were able to score both marks on this question. Several were able to give 1350 as the lower limit but often the upper limit was given as 1449. Other common errors were 1400/1500 and 1395/1405.
notes.7: Many candidates were able to give the correct answer. Others used Pythagoras’ theorem and rounded the third side to 4.6 which then led to an inaccurate answer for the angle. Some less able candidates did not understand trigonometry.
notes.10: 4 4 (a) This part was well answered. Common incorrect answers were 27 × 10 or 2.7 × 10 . (b) Very few correct answers were seen, with not many candidates realising that they had to divide by 2 to calculate the mean. Some scored 1 mark for figures 457 or 9.14 × 10 . 5 8
notes.11: Few candidates scored full marks as they were unable to deal with a mixed angle situation of a quadrilateral and an isosceles triangle. A lack of knowledge of angle properties was apparent. Several were able to work out 112° but could not go any further. Some thought angle x was 112. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0580 Mathematics June 2015
notes.13: Only a few of the more able candidates answered this correctly and then rounding was often incorrect, as many hadn’t rounded to two decimal places. 1.252 ÷ 2 and 1.252 × 2 were often seen.
notes.14: This fractions question was answered very well with nearly all candidates showing clear working. Decimals were only very occasionally seen as was inverting the wrong fraction. Many candidates were able to demonstrate an understanding of the common denominator method. 27
notes.15: This was a rather more challenging linear equation than is often seen. Many candidates expanded the brackets but then had problems re-arranging the algebraic terms. Often a correct −5 x = −14 led to x = −2.8. Answer 2.8
notes.16: The reduction of $17.50 was given by some candidates as the answer. Many did not know how to calculate a percentage reduction, some using 67.5 as the denominator. Some candidates were able to earn 1 mark for 79.4.

notes.12a: The majority of candidates were able to indicate both lines of symmetry. A very small number also added diagonal lines.
notes.12b: This part was generally answered correctly, with a small number giving the answer 4.
notes.18a: This was generally correctly answered but, as in previous questions, not rounding correctly let many candidates down. Many correctly found 0.85358 but then rounded to 0.9 rather than the two significant figures the question required. Some candidates didn’t show any working and only wrote 0.9 which meant 2 marks were lost. Some less able candidates scored 1 mark for either a correct numerator or denominator.
notes.18b: This was generally correctly answered , with the majority of those not scoring 2 marks being able to gain 1 for only 1 value in the wrong order.
notes.19a: Although some candidates gave the correct answer of 67, some had missed the key word in the question “ the prime number” and had written more than one number. A significant number appeared not to be familiar with the term prime as 63 and 65 were often seen.
notes.19b: Those who understood how to do this question generally wrote the correct answer. Others made an attempt but often did not go far enough leaving the answer as 2 × 3 × 9.
notes.19c: Although some candidates were able to give the correct answer, many were confused between HCF and LCM . Some gave common factors such as 2, 3 or 9.
notes.20a: This was generally well answered, although many candidates did not use π , with 18 × 12 = 216 being a common incorrect answer. Others calculated the volume using 2 π r h .
notes.20bi: This part was not well answered with many candidates calculating the volume. A significant number had not realised that 4 faces were not the same and 2 × 14 × 8 + 4 × 20 × 14 was common incorrect working.
notes.20bii: Again few correct answers were seen. Multiplying by ten rather than a hundred was seen the most often. Other candidates divided or multiplied by various powers of ten. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0580 Mathematics June 2015
